stories.title: A New Friend at the Library
stories.passage:
Mia is twelve years old. She lives in a small town with her mother and her brother, Leo. On Saturday morning, Mia goes to the town library. She likes books about animals and space.

At the library, she sees a boy near the door. He has a blue bag and a book in his hand.

“Hello,” says Mia. “Are you new here?”

“Yes,” says the boy. “My name is Adam. I am from another town.”

“Welcome! I am Mia. Do you like reading?”

“Yes, I do. I like adventure stories.”

Mia shows Adam the children's book section. They find a book about a young explorer. They sit at a table and read the first pages together.

At twelve o'clock, Adam says, “Thank you. This library is very nice.”

“You are welcome,” says Mia. “See you next Saturday!”

Where does Mia go on Saturday morning?
Who is Leo?

Where is Adam from?

What book do they find?

Is the library noisy or quiet? What does the story tell you?
Write one sentence describing Mia.

stories.title: The Missing Lunchbox
stories.passage:
Tom has a red lunchbox. Every school day, he puts an apple, a sandwich and a bottle of water inside it. On Tuesday, he arrives at school and puts his bag under his desk.

At lunchtime, Tom opens his bag. His lunchbox is not there.

“Oh no!” he says. “Where is my lunch?”

His friend Sara asks, “Did you leave it at home?”

“I don't think so,” Tom answers.

They look under the desk and beside the classroom door. Then Sara sees a red box on the teacher's table.

“Is that yours?” she asks.

Tom looks at it. “Yes! I put it there when I came into the classroom.”

The teacher smiles. “Here you are, Tom. Next time, put your lunchbox in your bag.”

“Thank you,” says Tom. He shares his apple with Sara.

What three things does he usually put inside it?
Which day does the story happen?
Where does Tom put his bag?

Why is it on the teacher's table?
What does Tom share with Sara?
What advice does the teacher give?

stories.title: A Weekend Without the Internet
stories.passage:
Last weekend, Nora's family had a problem with their internet connection. On Saturday morning, Nora wanted to watch a cooking video, but the page did not open. Her brother Sami tried to restart the router. It still did not work.

At first, everyone felt annoyed. Their father suggested spending the day outside. The family walked to a nearby park. Nora took photographs of flowers, Sami played football, and their parents sat under a tree and talked.

Later, they visited a small market and bought fresh vegetables. At home, Nora helped her mother prepare dinner. They made vegetable soup and a large salad.

On Sunday, the internet was working again. Nora watched her cooking video, but she also realised something important: a day without the internet could be enjoyable.

stories.title: A Better Way to Travel
stories.passage:
Daniel lives outside the city centre. For years, he travelled to work by car. The journey usually took forty minutes, but traffic sometimes made it much longer. He also spent a lot of money on petrol and parking.

One month ago, Daniel decided to try the train. The station is a ten-minute walk from his home. The train is usually faster than driving during the morning rush hour, and Daniel can read while he travels.

There are a few disadvantages. The train can be crowded, and sometimes it arrives late. However, Daniel now feels less stressed. He also walks more because he does not drive from door to door.

Daniel has not sold his car. He still uses it when he visits his parents in the countryside. For everyday travel, though, the train is his first choice.

stories.title: The Repair Café
stories.passage:
When Amira moved to a new neighbourhood, she noticed that many people threw away small household objects. A lamp stopped working, a chair became loose, or a radio made a strange noise. Often, the objects could be repaired, but their owners did not know how.

Amira had learned basic repair skills from her grandfather. She suggested organising a monthly repair café in the community hall. At first, only four people came. They repaired a desk lamp, a broken toy and two bicycles.

The following month, the event attracted more visitors. A retired electrician offered to help, while a local student designed a poster. The organisers created a simple booking system so that volunteers could prepare the right tools.

The repair café did more than save objects. People exchanged skills, met neighbours and discussed ways to reduce waste. Amira was pleased, but she understood that the project would only survive if more volunteers shared the work. She began training new helpers instead of trying to do everything herself.

stories.title: The Message That Arrived Too Late
stories.passage:
Ethan had been preparing a presentation for a regional science competition. His team had built a small device that measured the moisture in soil and sent the readings to a mobile phone. They wanted to demonstrate how the device could help gardeners use water more efficiently.

The night before the competition, Ethan discovered that one chart in the presentation contained incorrect figures. He corrected the data and sent the updated file to his teammates. Unfortunately, he attached the wrong version.

The next morning, the team opened the presentation at the venue and noticed the error. They had only twenty minutes before their turn. Instead of blaming Ethan, the team divided the work. One student checked the measurements, another updated the slides, and Ethan practised explaining the results.

Their presentation began on time. The judges asked difficult questions, especially about how the device would perform in different types of soil. The team admitted that they had tested only two soil types and explained what they planned to test next.

They did not win first prize, but one judge praised their honesty and practical thinking. Ethan learned that preparation matters, but so does responding calmly when plans fail.

3. What was the purpose of the device?

7. What limitation did the judges ask about?
8. How did the team respond to the limitation?
9. Did the team win first prize?

stories.title: The City That Reclaimed Its River
stories.passage:
For decades, the river that crossed Bellford was treated as a boundary rather than a public asset. Warehouses and car parks occupied much of its banks, while sections of the waterway were hidden behind concrete walls. Residents could see the river from a bridge, but few had a reason to spend time beside it.

That began to change when a group of residents, engineers and local businesses proposed a river restoration programme. The initial plan was controversial. Some business owners feared that construction would disrupt deliveries, while residents questioned whether public money should be spent on landscaping when other services needed investment.

The project team responded by publishing cost estimates, flood-risk assessments and a phased construction schedule. It also held public meetings where residents could challenge the proposals. Several design changes followed. A proposed ornamental fountain was removed, for example, and replaced with a wetland area intended to absorb excess rainwater.

Five years later, the river corridor includes walking paths, native plants and small public spaces. The wetland has helped manage stormwater, although maintenance remains expensive. Local shops report more visitors, but it would be difficult to attribute every increase in business to the river project alone.

The programme is often described as a success, yet its most valuable result may be institutional rather than visual: residents now expect major public projects to explain their evidence, costs and trade-offs.



1. How was the river treated before the programme?
2. Why were residents unable to enjoy the river easily?
3. Identify two groups that had concerns about the proposal and explain their concerns.
4. How did the project team respond to criticism?
5. Why was the fountain replaced by a wetland?
6. What environmental function does the wetland perform?
7. Why does the writer qualify the claim about increased business?
8. What does the final paragraph suggest is the programme's institutional legacy?

4. To say that one thing caused another: **attribute / reclaim / maintain**

stories.title: The Algorithm at the Admissions Desk
stories.passage:
A university introduced an automated system to help staff review scholarship applications. The system ranked applications according to academic results, extracurricular activities and written statements. Administrators expected it to reduce delays and make the process more consistent.

During the first year, the average review time fell. Staff also reported that the system helped them identify applications that might otherwise have been overlooked. However, an internal audit found that applicants from some schools were consistently receiving lower scores for leadership experience. The schools in question offered fewer organised extracurricular activities, even though their students often contributed to family businesses or community projects.

The university paused the system and invited students, teachers and admissions officers to examine the scoring criteria. The review panel concluded that the software had not been deliberately designed to disadvantage particular groups. Nevertheless, the data used to train and test it reflected unequal opportunities.

The university revised the criteria and introduced a human review stage for borderline cases. It also began collecting information about different forms of responsibility and contribution. The new process is slower than the original automated model, but administrators argue that speed is not the only measure of quality.

The case illustrates a broader challenge: a system can apply the same rule to everyone and still produce unfair outcomes when people's starting conditions are unequal.

2. Name two benefits reported during the first year.
3. Which applicants were disadvantaged by the scoring approach?
4. Why did the scoring criteria fail to recognise some students' experience?
5. Did the review panel find deliberate discrimination in the software's design?
6. What was the deeper problem identified by the panel?
7. Name two changes made to the process.
8. Why might the revised system be slower?
9. Explain the distinction between applying the same rule and achieving a fair outcome.
10. What evidence would you want to examine before judging whether the revised system is fair?

stories.title: The Archive of Ordinary Things
stories.passage:
When the municipal archive announced that it was collecting objects from residents, the response was unexpectedly enthusiastic. The curators had not asked for rare paintings or historically important documents. They wanted ordinary things: a bus ticket, a handwritten shopping list, a repaired kettle, a school badge, a recipe card stained with oil.

The project began with a question that sounded almost trivial: what would future generations misunderstand about everyday life if they encountered only official records? Government reports might describe a housing development, but they would rarely reveal how neighbours shared tools, how families adapted recipes when ingredients were scarce, or how children invented games in unfinished streets.

Each donated object came with a short account. Some accounts contradicted one another. Two residents remembered the same street market as either a lively centre of community life or a place where noise and congestion made daily routines difficult. The curators decided not to resolve every disagreement. Instead, they recorded the differences, noting that memory is selective and that a public archive should not manufacture a single authorised version of the past.

The collection soon became more than a store of objects. It provided a setting for conversations between generations. Older residents explained how they repaired household goods; younger visitors described how digital tools had altered their habits. Neither group was presented as a model of virtue or decline.

The archive's director argued that ordinary objects are valuable not because they tell a complete story, but because they expose the gaps in the stories societies tell about themselves.

2. What limitation of official records does the project seek to address?
3. Explain the contrast between the two residents' memories of the market.
4. Why did the curators preserve conflicting accounts instead of choosing one?
5. What does the phrase “single authorised version of the past” imply?
6. How does the archive avoid idealising either older or younger generations?
7. Explain the director's final claim in your own words.
8. Identify one assumption about memory that underpins the project.

stories.title: The Quiet Cost of Convenience
stories.passage:
The language of convenience has become so familiar that it can obscure the systems required to produce it. A parcel arrives the day after an order is placed; a meal appears at the door; a digital service responds instantly. From the customer's perspective, friction has been removed. Yet the friction has not necessarily disappeared. It may have been transferred to workers, suppliers, local infrastructure or the environment.

This does not mean that convenience is inherently undesirable. Rapid delivery can be essential for medical supplies, and digital services can make information accessible to people who would otherwise face significant barriers. The difficulty arises when speed is treated as an unconditional good and the costs of achieving it are excluded from the calculation.

A more complete assessment would ask not simply whether a service is fast, but who absorbs the pressure that makes it fast. Are workers given realistic schedules? Are suppliers paid in a way that allows them to maintain quality? Does the delivery model increase congestion? Can customers choose a slower option without being penalised?

The challenge for organisations is to design convenience that is not dependent on making its costs invisible. That may involve offering delivery windows rather than promises of instant arrival, publishing meaningful service standards, or allowing users to select options that balance speed, price and environmental impact.

The most responsible service may not be the one that removes every delay. It may be the one that makes its trade-offs visible and gives people a genuine choice.



1. What does the writer mean by the transfer of “friction”?
2. Why does the writer avoid claiming that convenience is always harmful?
3. What assumption is challenged in the second paragraph?
4. Identify four questions that a more complete assessment should ask.
5. Explain the phrase “making its costs invisible.”
6. What examples of responsible design are proposed?
7. What is the central argument of the final paragraph?
8. Identify two rhetorical techniques used to develop the argument.
9. What is the writer's attitude towards speed?

stories.title: The Committee of Future Readers
stories.passage:
The committee had been convened to decide what should be preserved when the old civic building was converted into a public learning centre. The building's supporters spoke of continuity; its critics spoke of opportunity. Both sides claimed to be defending the public interest, though they meant different things by it.

The architect presented a plan that retained the entrance hall and the staircase but replaced most internal walls. The proposal was efficient, accessible and comparatively inexpensive. A local historian objected that the building's significance lay not in its façade but in the arrangement of rooms, which had shaped the institution's public rituals for nearly a century.

A student representative asked a question that unsettled the room: “If we preserve the building as it was, whose experience are we preserving?” The historian acknowledged that the old arrangement had excluded some residents. The architect, in turn, conceded that efficiency alone could not determine what deserved to survive.

The committee postponed its decision. It requested an account of the building's changing uses, an accessibility assessment and a series of workshops with groups whose experiences had been absent from the official record. The delay was criticised as indecision. Yet the chair argued that a decision made quickly would merely conceal the assumptions on which it rested.

Months later, the committee recommended retaining selected spatial features while documenting those that would be removed. It also proposed a public exhibition that would present conflicting accounts rather than harmonise them into a single narrative.

The final report did not claim to have discovered the building's one true meaning. It argued, more modestly, that preservation is not the suspension of change but a public negotiation over which traces of the past should remain legible in the future.



1. Explain the competing meanings of “continuity” and “opportunity” in the opening paragraph.
2. Why does the historian consider the arrangement of rooms significant?
3. What does the student's question reveal about the assumptions behind preservation?
4. How does the historian's acknowledgement complicate their original position?
5. Why is the architect's concession important?
6. Distinguish between postponement as indecision and postponement as a deliberate method.
7. What does the phrase “whose experience are we preserving?” imply about historical representation?
8. Explain “make assumptions legible” in the context of the chair's argument.
9. Why might the committee's final recommendation be considered a compromise without being a simple midpoint?
10. Interpret the final sentence. What theory of preservation does it propose?
11. Identify an unresolved tension in the story.
12. Write a 50-word abstract of the story.

stories.title: The Price of a Perfect Forecast
stories.passage:
The forecasting office had become famous for its accuracy, although the director disliked the word. A forecast, she insisted, was not a promise about the future but a disciplined statement about what might happen under specified conditions. The distinction was obvious to specialists and almost invisible to the public.

When the office predicted a severe water shortage, the announcement was widely interpreted as certainty. Households reduced consumption; businesses postponed expansion; local authorities accelerated infrastructure projects. Some of these measures proved beneficial. Others were costly, and a few became unnecessary when rainfall exceeded the model's central estimate.

The director was asked whether the office had been wrong. She replied that the model had described a range of plausible outcomes and that the realised result had fallen within that range. Her answer was technically defensible, but it did little to address the public's sense that a warning had been presented as a verdict.

A review found that the technical report had included uncertainty intervals, assumptions and alternative scenarios. The public summary, however, had reduced these qualifications to a single headline. The simplification had been made to improve clarity, but it had also changed the practical meaning of the forecast.

The office revised its communication policy. Every public warning would now distinguish the most likely outcome from the plausible range, identify the assumptions that mattered most, and explain which decisions were robust across several scenarios. The director also accepted that uncertainty should not be relegated to a footnote: it was part of the result.

The episode changed the office's understanding of accuracy. A forecast could be statistically sound and still mislead if its uncertainty was communicated poorly. Precision, the director concluded, was not merely a property of numbers. It was also an obligation owed to the people who acted on them.



1. Why does the director dislike describing forecasts as accurate?
2. What distinction does she make between a forecast and a promise?
3. How did the public interpret the water-shortage announcement?
4. Which consequences of the warning were beneficial, and which were costly?
5. Why was the director's answer technically defensible?
6. Why did the answer fail to satisfy public concerns?
7. Where did the review locate the main communication failure?
8. How did the public summary alter the meaning of the technical report?
9. What changes did the office make to its communication policy?
10. What does it mean for a decision to be “robust across several scenarios”?
11. Explain the final claim that precision is an obligation.
12. Is the story primarily about modelling, communication, public trust or all three? Defend your view.



Compare the two stories in this C2 section.

- How do both stories challenge the idea that expert decisions are purely technical?
- What role does public interpretation play?
- How do the stories treat uncertainty?
